definition.text: An organism's position in a food web, counted as the number of feeding steps it is from the start of the chain.

facts.text: Level 1 is primary producers such as plants, level 2 herbivores, level 3 or higher carnivores, and apex predators typically sit at level 4 or 5.
Organisms get food in three basic ways: as producers, consumers or decomposers.
Herbivores are primary consumers, carnivores that eat them are secondary consumers, and carnivores that eat carnivores are tertiary consumers.
Raymond Lindeman developed the concept in 1942, building on August Thienemann's 1926 terms producers, consumers and reducers.
Consumers convert on average only about 10% of the energy in their food into their own tissue, so food chains rarely exceed 5 or 6 levels.
Plants turn about 1% of the sunlight they receive into chemical energy, so only about 0.001% of it ends up in a tertiary consumer.
Fish at higher trophic levels usually fetch more money, which can lead to overfishing at those levels.
Humans have a mean trophic level of about 2.21, about the same as a pig or an anchovy.

title: Fractional trophic level

definition.text: A trophic level that need not be a whole number, because many organisms feed at more than one level.

facts.text: A consumer's trophic level is one plus the diet-weighted average trophic level of what it eats.
Most fish and other marine consumers fall between 2.0 and 5.0; 5.0 occurs in apex predators such as polar bears and orcas.
Trophic level can be measured from stable nitrogen isotopes in tissues, which rise about 3–4‰ at each level.

distinct_from: Mean trophic level of fisheries catch

title: Mean trophic level of fisheries catch

definition.text: The average trophic level of all the fish caught in an area or ecosystem in a given year, used to track fishing pressure.

facts.text: Early reports found steep declines in it, a process called fishing down the food web.
Pauly and colleagues report it peaked at 3.4 in 1970 in the northwest and west-central Atlantic and fell to 2.9 by 1994, as catches shifted from cod and haddock to shrimp and herring.
Pauly and others built the Fisheries in Balance (FiB) index in 2000 to check whether falling trophic levels are matched by rising catches.

contested_note: Later work found mean trophic levels in catches and surveys have not declined globally, suggesting fishing down the food web is not worldwide.

definition.text: An interaction linking three trophic levels at once, such as plant, herbivore and predator.

facts.text: Studying only two levels at a time can mislead, because plants and predators together can shape herbivore population growth.
Plant shape can change how well a plant resists herbivores by affecting the herbivores' enemies.

definition.text: The science of conserving nature and Earth's biodiversity, aiming to protect species, habitats and ecosystems from excessive extinction.

facts.text: It is interdisciplinary, drawing on natural and social sciences and on natural resource management, and reaches into law, economics and philosophy.
The field took its name from the First International Conference on Research in Conservation Biology, held in 1978 in La Jolla, California.
Because natural systems are declining fast, it is often called a 'discipline with a deadline'.
Conservation is either in-situ, protecting a species in its natural habitat, or ex-situ, outside it, such as in gene banks.
Conservation biologists have begun working with economists to measure nature's wealth and services, an accounting approach called natural capital.
The global extinction rate may be about 1,000 times higher than the natural background rate.
Some conservationists follow a resource ethic of the greatest good for the most people, while others argue nature has intrinsic value apart from its usefulness.

definition.text: A species with narrow ecological needs whose condition is watched as a sign of an ecosystem's health.

facts.text: Amphibians, with permeable skin and ties to wetlands, are very sensitive to environmental harm and can act as a 'miner's canary'.
They are monitored to detect damage from pollution or other human activity, and can guide changes in practice such as forestry methods.
Monitoring several indicators, from genes to landscapes, is generally recommended.

definition.text: A species whose protection also shelters many other species and habitats because it needs a large area.

facts.text: The monarch butterfly migrates across North America through many ecosystems, so protecting it protects much else.
Umbrella species often double as flagship species, such as the giant panda or tiger, that capture public attention.
Conservation bias towards flagship species can sometimes threaten other species of greater concern.

definition.text: A step-by-step way of choosing and designing reserves to protect the highest-priority biodiversity efficiently.

facts.text: Margules and Pressey set out six linked stages, from compiling biodiversity data and setting goals to selecting new areas and maintaining their value.
Planners generally use geographic information systems to support decisions.

definition.text: A summary of the main threats to biodiversity: habitat loss, invasive species, pollution, human population and overharvesting.

facts.text: The primary threats are habitat destruction, such as deforestation and urban growth, and overexploitation, such as wildlife trade.
